items.q: A 4-year-old child presents with short stature, dense and brittle bones, open anterior fontanelle, and delayed eruption of teeth. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the CTSK gene encoding cathepsin K, leading to impaired degradation of organic matrix during bone resorption. Which of the following conditions is caused by this specific defect?
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a mutation in cathepsin K (CTSK), a lysosomal cysteine protease secreted by osteoclasts to digest collagen during bone resorption. Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency causes osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis, while RUNX2 mutation causes cleidocranial dysplasia.
items.note: Accurate, highly specific, and standard superspeciality exam question based on bone cell biochemistry and genetic dysplasias.

items.q: In normal mature long bones, cortical blood flow is centrifugal (inside-out). Following a displaced diaphyseal fracture treated with intramedullary reaming, which of the following changes in cortical blood supply occurs?
o: Centrifugal flow increases due to hyperaemia of the nutrient artery
Flow becomes centripetal, as periosteal vessels supply the cortex
Endosteal blood supply increases five-fold while periosteal flow ceases
Flow becomes static due to complete permanent thrombosis of all cortical vessels
items.e: Normal cortical blood flow is centrifugal because the high-pressure nutrient artery system supplies the inner two-thirds of the cortex. Displaced fractures and intramedullary reaming temporarily destroy the endosteal supply, shifting blood flow to a centripetal (outside-in) direction where the periosteal supply dominates until endosteal regeneration occurs.
items.note: Classic applied basic science topic tested frequently in orthopaedic entrance examinations.

items.q: A 13-year-old boy presents with painful limping and an antalgic gait. Radiographs reveal a Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE). Mechanically, the slippage in SCFE, as well as most Salter-Harris physeal fractures, typically occurs through which zone of the growth plate?
items.e: Both Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) and common physeal fractures (Salter-Harris types I and II) pass through the hypertrophic zone (specifically the zone of provisional calcification). This zone has enlarged chondrocytes with decreased matrix and low mechanical resistance, making it the weakest region of the physis.
items.note: High-yield core topic with unambiguous consensus in Campbell's and standard paediatric orthopaedic texts.

items.q: The International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF) and the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) recommend standard reference markers to monitor response to osteoporosis treatment. Which pair of markers is recommended?
items.e: The IOF and IFCC recommend serum P1NP (procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide) as the standard reference marker for bone formation and serum CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen) as the standard reference marker for bone resorption. These markers reflect systemic bone turnover and change rapidly in response to treatment.
items.note: Factually accurate standard international recommendation explicitly stated in bone biology reference notes.

items.q: Which of the following non-collagenous proteins is the most abundant in the organic bone matrix, undergoes vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, is secreted by osteoblasts upon stimulation by 1,25(OH)2D, and serves as a serum marker of bone formation?
items.e: Osteocalcin (bone Gla protein) is the most abundant non-collagenous matrix protein in bone. It is produced by osteoblasts, undergoes vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, is stimulated by 1,25(OH)2D, attracts osteoclasts, and serves as a clinical biomarker of bone formation.
items.note: Standard high-yield biochemistry question in bone matrix biology.

items.q: A clinical investigator is examining the target cells of parathyroid hormone (PTH) in bone remodelling. Which cell type involved in bone turnover lacks PTH/PTHrP receptors (PTH1R) and responds to PTH only indirectly?
items.e: Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors. Parathyroid hormone stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption indirectly by binding to PTH1R on osteoblasts and osteocytes, which stimulates RANKL production and suppresses osteoprotegerin (OPG), driving osteoclast differentiation and activation.
items.note: Fundamental physiology question testing cellular signaling pathways in bone remodeling.

items.q: According to the bioelectric properties of bone, when a long bone undergoes mechanical bending, which electrical state develops on the compression side and what cellular action does it induce?
o: Electronegative charge; stimulates osteoblastic bone formation
Electropositive charge; stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption
Electronegative charge; stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption
Electropositive charge; stimulates osteoblastic bone formation
items.e: Bone exhibits piezoelectric and bioelectric properties under mechanical stress: the side under compression becomes electronegative, which stimulates osteoblastic bone formation. Conversely, the side under tension becomes electropositive, stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer question assessing piezoelectricity and cellular adaptation to stress.

items.q: Which of the following biochemical and physical changes is characteristically observed in normal physiological cartilage ageing, in contrast to early osteoarthritis?
o: Increased water content in the extracellular matrix
Increased keratan sulfate content relative to chondroitin-4 sulfate
items.e: In physiological cartilage ageing, water content and chondroitin-4 sulfate decrease while keratan sulfate increases, causing the chondroitin to keratan sulfate ratio to fall and tissue stiffness (modulus of elasticity) to rise. Conversely, early osteoarthritis is characterized by increased water content, increased chondroitin-4 sulfate, increased permeability, and decreased modulus of elasticity.
items.note: Accurate comparison between physiological ageing and early osteoarthritis directly based on standard reference facts.

items.q: A 30-year-old orthopaedic researcher is studying the zonal organization of human articular cartilage. Which layer is characterized by having the highest collagen and water content, the lowest proteoglycan content, and collagen fibrils aligned parallel to the joint surface?
items.e: The superficial (tangential) zone comprises 10-20% of articular cartilage thickness and contains flattened chondrocytes, the highest water and collagen concentration, and the lowest proteoglycan content. Collagen fibrils in this zone are oriented parallel to the joint surface to resist shear stress.
items.note: Clear, single-best-answer question testing cartilage zonal architecture.

items.q: A 42-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis undergoes a synovial biopsy. Pathological examination reveals prominent hyperplasia of the synovial lining, with aggressive invasion into articular cartilage. Which cell type in the synovium is a fibroblast-like cell of mesenchymal origin responsible for producing hyaluronic acid and lubricin, as well as serving as the key effector cell of rheumatoid pannus?
items.e: Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like cells derived from mesenchymal lineage that synthesize hyaluronic acid, lubricin, collagen, and fibronectin. They also act as the principal effector cells in rheumatoid pannus that invade and degrade articular cartilage.
items.note: Factually accurate histological distinction between Type A and Type B synoviocytes.

items.q: A 24-year-old athlete undergoes microfracture (Steadman technique) for a 1.5 cm² full-thickness chondral defect of the medial femoral condyle. What is the predominant collagen type present in the repair tissue that fills the defect following this marrow stimulation procedure?
items.e: Microfracture breaches the subchondral plate to form a marrow clot rich in mesenchymal stem cells, which heals the defect with fibrocartilage. Fibrocartilage is dominated mechanically by Type I collagen, making it inferior to normal hyaline cartilage (which is dominated by Type II collagen).
items.note: High-yield exam fact regarding repair tissue type after microfracture.

items.q: A 32-year-old male presents with recurrent swelling and mechanical pain in his right knee. Synovial fluid aspiration yields dark brown, haemorrhagic fluid without crystals or bacteria. MRI of the knee reveals diffuse synovial thickening with low signal intensity on both T1- and T2-weighted images, displaying marked 'blooming' artifact on gradient-echo sequences. Which of the following genetic alterations is pathognomonic for this condition?
items.e: The clinical and MRI features (low T1/T2 signal and gradient-echo blooming due to haemosiderin) are characteristic of pigmented villonodular synovitis (tenosynovial giant cell tumour). This benign neoplastic proliferation is driven by a CSF1 gene translocation causing CSF1 overexpression that recruits non-neoplastic macrophages.
items.note: Accurately integrates clinical, imaging, and molecular pathology facts.

items.q: In the catabolic cascade leading to matrix degradation in osteoarthritis, which specific enzyme is primarily responsible for direct cleavage of Type II collagen fibrils?
items.e: MMP-13 (collagenase-3) is the primary matrix metalloproteinase responsible for degrading Type II collagen in articular cartilage. Aggrecan breakdown is predominantly mediated by aggrecanases (ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5).
items.note: Directly tests the specific catabolic enzyme responsible for Type II collagen breakdown.

items.q: A 22-year-old pitcher undergoes shoulder arthroscopy. Postoperatively, a continuous intra-articular pain pump delivering a local anaesthetic is used. Weeks later, he develops rapid, severe loss of joint space due to widespread chondrocyte death (post-arthroscopic glenohumeral chondrolysis). Which agent is classically associated with this chondrotoxic complication?
items.e: Continuous intra-articular infusion of local anaesthetics, particularly bupivacaine via post-arthroscopic pain pumps, is direct and potent chondrotoxicity that can lead to rapid post-arthroscopic glenohumeral chondrolysis.
items.note: Classic orthopaedic basic science/clinical correlation question.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient with severe left hip osteoarthritis is evaluated for conservative gait modifications prior to joint replacement. Which of the following actions will INCREASE the joint reaction force across the affected hip joint?
o: Using a walking cane in the contralateral hand
Carrying a heavy briefcase in the contralateral hand
Leaning the trunk over the affected side during stance (Trendelenburg lurch)
Carrying a heavy load in the ipsilateral hand
items.e: Carrying a load in the contralateral hand increases the body weight moment arm relative to the hip, thereby requiring a greater abductor muscle force and increasing the overall joint reaction force (JRF). Conversely, using a cane in the contralateral hand reduces hip JRF by up to 40–60%, and carrying loads in the ipsilateral hand or leaning over the affected hip (Trendelenburg lurch) reduces abductor muscle demand and JRF.
items.note: Accurate biomechanical concept regarding hip joint reaction forces and lever arms.

items.q: During the processing of highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) for total joint replacement components, remelting the polymer above its melting point eliminates free radicals but results in which mechanical drawback?
o: Reduction in fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength
Complete loss of resistance to adhesive and abrasive wear
Inability to eliminate residual free radicals, leading to rapid shelf oxidation
Drastic increase in the Young's modulus above that of cortical bone
items.e: Remelting HXLPE above its melting point eliminates residual free radicals created during gamma irradiation, thereby preventing oxidation, but it reduces the material's fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength. In contrast, annealing below the melting point preserves mechanical properties but leaves residual free radicals.
items.note: Factually correct polymer material property concept commonly tested in orthopaedic biomaterials.

items.q: During an open bone biopsy of the femoral shaft, creating a rectangular longitudinal slot (open-section defect) in the cortex reduces which mechanical property of the bone most drastically compared with a simple round drill hole?
items.e: An open-section defect, such as a longitudinal slot or cortical window, drastically reduces the torsional strength of bone by well over half (up to 90%), far more than a round or oval hole. Biopsy defects should have rounded ends to minimize stress concentration.
items.note: Standard orthopaedic basic science principle on stress risers and open-section defects in bone.

items.q: In polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement, which component is added to the liquid monomer mixture specifically to act as a stabilizer and prevent premature polymerization during storage?
items.e: Hydroquinone is included in the liquid monomer as a stabilizer/inhibitor to prevent premature polymerization during storage. Benzoyl peroxide (in the powder) is the initiator, DMPT (in the liquid) is the accelerator, and barium sulfate is a radiopacifier.
items.note: Completely accurate chemical composition knowledge for bone cement.

items.q: Which of the following modifications provides the most substantial increase in the overall construct stiffness of a unilateral linear external fixator?
o: Increasing the diameter of the Schanz pins
Placing the connecting bar further away from the skin surface
Decreasing the distance between the two pins within the same main bone fragment
Using a single connecting bar instead of two stacked bars
items.e: Increasing the pin diameter is the single most effective way to increase external fixator stiffness because pin bending stiffness is proportional to its radius to the fourth power (r^4). Bringing the bar closer to bone and placing pins far apart within each fragment also increase stiffness.
items.note: Factually precise biomechanical principle regarding external fixators.

items.q: According to Perren's strain theory, what is the expected tissue response and fracture healing pattern when the interfragmentary strain across a fracture gap is maintained between 2% and 10%?
o: Primary bone healing by cutting cones without callus
Secondary bone healing with callus formation
Formation of granulation tissue only, resulting in non-union
Complete absence of periosteal reaction and avascular necrosis
items.e: According to Perren's interfragmentary strain theory, strain under 2% leads to primary (direct) bone healing by cutting cones under absolute stability, strain between 2% and 10% produces secondary (indirect) bone healing with callus under relative stability, and strain exceeding 10% leads to non-union.
items.note: Standard core concept in fracture mechanics and bone healing.

items.q: Which of the following orthopedic implant biomaterials has a Young's modulus of elasticity that is closest to that of human cortical bone (~15–20 GPa)?
items.e: Among the listed metals and ceramics, titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) has the lowest Young's modulus (~110 GPa), making it the closest to cortical bone (~15–20 GPa) and thereby reducing stress shielding compared to stiffer metals like cobalt-chromium (~210–230 GPa) or stainless steel (~190–200 GPa).
items.note: Factually accurate ordering of Young's modulus among orthopaedic metallic and ceramic materials.

items.q: A patient with a metal-on-polyethylene total hip arthroplasty (CoCr femoral head on a titanium alloy stem) develops a pseudotumor. Laboratory evaluation reveals significantly elevated serum cobalt levels relative to chromium levels. Which corrosion mechanism at the modular head-neck taper interface is responsible for this condition?
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC, or trunnionosis) occurs at modular head-neck taper junctions due to a combination of fretting (micromotion breaking the passive oxide layer) and crevice corrosion. It characteristically results in elevated serum cobalt levels disproportionate to chromium and can lead to adverse local tissue reactions (pseudotumors).
items.note: Accurate description of trunnionosis and corrosion mechanics in modern total joint arthroplasty.

items.q: During a micro-neurolysis procedure under high magnification, a surgeon inadvertently makes a small longitudinal incision through the perineurium of a peripheral nerve fascicle. Which of the following is the immediate structural consequence of this injury?
o: Immediate loss of distal nerve electrical excitability
Direct axonal sprouting outside the sheath
Rapid Wallerian degeneration of the distal nerve segment
items.e: The perineurium maintains intrafascicular pressure, serves as the blood-nerve barrier, and provides the main tensile strength of the nerve. Disrupting the perineurium leads to herniation of fascicular contents.
items.note: Accurate basic science concept directly tested in superspeciality exams; options are clear and mutually exclusive.

items.q: A 24-year-old motor-cyclist sustains a traumatic brachial plexus traction injury causing complete sensory loss in the C5 and C6 dermatomes. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies performed 4 weeks later demonstrate a normal, preserved sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) for the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve despite total clinical anaesthesia. Which injury pattern does this electrophysiological finding confirm?
o: Postganglionic nerve transection distal to the dorsal root ganglion
Preganglionic root avulsion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
Neurapraxic conduction block across the trunk
items.e: In a preganglionic root avulsion, the sensory cell body in the dorsal root ganglion remains intact and connected to the peripheral axon. Therefore, the peripheral SNAP remains preserved despite total clinical sensory loss.
items.note: Classic and high-yield electrodiagnostic principle in brachial plexus trauma.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon plans a nerve transfer to restore shoulder abduction and external rotation in a patient with a upper trunk brachial plexus injury. Which donor nerve is classically transferred to the suprascapular nerve for this purpose?
o: Ulnar nerve fascicle to flexor carpi ulnaris
Radial nerve branch to the long head of triceps
Anterior interosseous nerve branch to pronator quadratus
items.e: Transfer of the distal spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) to the suprascapular nerve is used to restore shoulder abduction and external rotation in proximal plexus injuries, while preserving upper trapezius innervation.
items.note: Standard reconstructive nerve transfer option and alignment match established surgical notes.

items.q: According to the sliding filament theory of skeletal muscle contraction, which zone or band within the sarcomere remains CONSTANT in length during concentric contraction?
items.e: The A band represents the total length of the thick myosin filaments and maintains a constant length during muscle contraction. The I band and H zone shorten as thin actin filaments slide past thick myosin filaments.
items.note: Basic muscle physiology question, accurate and unequivocally supported.

items.q: When applying local anaesthetics for peripheral nerve block, nerve fibres are blocked in a characteristic functional sequence based on diameter and myelination. Which of the following nerve fibre types is blocked FIRST?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block small, thinly myelinated or unmyelinated fibres first. The sequence of blockade is B (preganglionic autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch, pressure) > A-alpha (motor, proprioception).
items.note: Standard Erlanger-Gasser classification physiology question.

items.q: A sprinter experiences a sudden sharp pain in the posterior thigh during acceleration. Diagnostic imaging confirms an acute muscle strain at the myotendinous junction of the long head of biceps femoris. Which type of muscle contraction is primarily responsible for causing this strain injury?
items.e: Eccentric contraction generates the greatest peak forces within muscle tissue and is the main mechanism causing muscle strain injuries, predominantly occurring at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles rich in type II fibres.
items.note: High-yield sports orthopaedics concept.

items.q: During emergency open reduction and internal fixation under general anaesthesia with volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine, a patient experiences a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, masseter rigidity, and hyperthermia. This life-threatening reaction is caused by a mutation in which of the following proteins?
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the RYR1 gene (ryanodine receptor 1), causing uncontrolled sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release when exposed to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine.
items.note: Directly supported basic science and anaesthesia interface question.

items.q: An orthopaedic registrar evaluates a closed humeral shaft fracture with an acute complete radial nerve palsy. To distinguish neurapraxia from axonal injury using electromyography (EMG), how long after the initial injury should the baseline EMG study be performed?
items.e: Denervation features such as fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves require approximately 2 to 3 weeks (10 to 21 days) to develop on EMG. Delaying diagnostic EMG to 3 to 4 weeks allows accurate differentiation between neurapraxia and axonal injury.
items.note: Core electrodiagnosis timing question commonly assessed in exams.

items.q: A clinical investigator evaluates a novel serum biomarker for detecting prosthetic joint infection (PJI). In a preliminary study, the test demonstrated a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. When applied to a tertiary revision clinic with a high prevalence of PJI (20%) versus a community orthopaedic clinic with a low prevalence of PJI (2%), which of the following statistical parameters will remain UNCHANGED between the two settings?
o: Proportion of false-positive results in the population
items.e: Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios (LR+ and LR-) are intrinsic performance properties of a diagnostic test and do not change with disease prevalence. In contrast, predictive values (PPV and NPV) depend directly on disease prevalence; as prevalence rises, PPV rises and NPV falls.
items.note: Accurate, clear diagnostic test question directly derived from the reference notes.

items.q: A surgeon reviews hospital records to compare the 5-year implant survivorship of two different femoral stem designs used in patients who underwent total hip arthroplasty between 2010 and 2015. Surgical details and outcomes were gathered retrospectively from patient charts. According to the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS) hierarchy for therapeutic studies, what level of evidence does this study represent?
items.e: A retrospective comparative cohort study and a case-control study are classified as Level III evidence. Prospective comparative cohort studies represent Level II evidence, whereas non-comparative case series represent Level IV evidence.
items.note: Standard level of evidence question, fully aligned with JBJS hierarchy rules.

items.q: An investigator is analysing 15-year implant survivorship of a total knee arthroplasty system in an elderly cohort (mean age 78 years at index surgery). During long-term follow-up, a significant proportion of subjects die before requiring revision surgery. If the investigator performs a standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis treating death as a censored event, what is the effect on the estimated cumulative revision rate?
o: It overestimates the cumulative revision rate
It underestimates the cumulative revision rate
It eliminates loss to follow-up bias completely
It provides an unbiased adjusted hazard ratio
items.e: When death acts as a competing risk (preventing the event of interest, revision), standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis overestimates the cumulative revision rate because it assumes censored patients would experience revision at the same rate as surviving patients. To handle competing risks accurately in elderly populations, the cumulative incidence function (Fine and Gray) should be used.
items.note: Important statistical concept in joint registry and survivorship analysis.

items.q: In a randomised trial evaluating an antimicrobial incisional dressing in primary total knee arthroplasty, surgical site infection occurred in 5% of patients in the intervention group (experimental event rate) compared to 10% of patients receiving standard dressings (control event rate). What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) with the new dressing to prevent one additional surgical site infection?
items.e: Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) = Control Event Rate (CER) - Experimental Event Rate (EER) = 10% - 5% = 5% (0.05). Number Needed to Treat (NNT) = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.05 = 20.
items.note: Standard NNT calculation question based on clear formula.

items.q: An observational study demonstrates an association between heavy cigarette smoking and delayed bone healing in open tibial fractures. When evaluating whether this association represents a true causal relationship using the Bradford Hill criteria, which of the following is considered the ONLY essential criterion?
items.e: Among the Bradford Hill criteria for evaluating causality (strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy), temporality—the requirement that exposure must precede the outcome—is the only criterion that is strictly essential.
items.note: High-yield epidemiology concept explicitly noted as essential.

items.q: An orthopaedic research group is preparing a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing surgical fixation versus non-operative treatment for displaced clavicle fractures. Which reporting guideline and protocol registry are standard for this study design?
items.e: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses should be conducted and reported according to the PRISMA guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) and registered prospectively on the PROSPERO database. CONSORT is used for RCTs, STROBE for observational studies, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies.
items.note: Factually correct match of guidelines and databases for systematic reviews.

items.q: An investigator tests a novel osteoinductive bone graft substitute against standard autograft across 5 separate secondary clinical endpoints in a clinical trial. To control the overall Type I error rate (alpha) at 0.05 across these multiple comparisons, a Bonferroni correction is applied. What adjusted significance threshold (alpha) should be used for each individual endpoint?
items.e: Performing multiple statistical comparisons inflates the overall Type I (false positive) error rate. The Bonferroni correction adjusts for multiple testing by dividing the overall significance level (alpha = 0.05) by the number of comparisons made (5 tests), yielding an adjusted threshold of 0.05 / 5 = 0.010 per test.
items.note: Simple and clean mathematical/statistical application question.

items.q: During lateral fluoroscopy using a C-arm in the operating theatre, on which side of the patient should the surgeon stand to minimize occupational radiation scatter exposure?
o: Position relative to the C-arm does not affect scatter dose
Directly adjacent to the primary beam entrance
items.e: Compton radiation scatter is greatest on the X-ray tube (entrance) side of the patient. Therefore, during lateral fluoroscopy views, the surgeon should stand on the image intensifier/detector side to minimize occupational scatter dose.
items.note: Completely accurate, clear SBA format, fully supported by reference notes.

items.q: An MRI of the shoulder demonstrates high signal intensity in the supraspinatus tendon on short-TE (T1-weighted and proton density) sequences, which completely disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences. This finding is characteristic of which artefact?
items.e: Magic angle artefact occurs when collagen fibres are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the main magnetic field (B0), resulting in high signal intensity on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) that disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences.
items.note: High-yield MRI physics concept, standard and unambiguous.

items.q: Which of the following radiation-induced biological effects follows a linear no-threshold model, where the probability of occurrence—rather than its severity—increases with radiation dose?
items.e: Carcinogenesis is a stochastic effect governed by a linear no-threshold model, meaning any radiation dose carries a probability of effect, but severity is independent of dose. Cataracts, skin erythema, and sterility are deterministic effects with specific threshold doses.
items.note: Accurate distinction between stochastic and deterministic radiation effects.

items.q: A 40-year-old premenopausal female undergoes DEXA scanning for suspected secondary osteoporosis. Which metric should be evaluated, and what threshold defines a bone mineral density 'below the expected range for age'?
items.e: In premenopausal women, men under 50 years of age, and children, bone mineral density is evaluated using the Z-score (compared against age- and sex-matched controls). A Z-score of -2.0 or lower is defined as 'below the expected range for age'.
items.note: Standard WHO/ISCD guidelines on bone densitometry reporting.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient presents with multiple osteolytic skeletal lesions. A Tc-99m MDP bone scan reveals photopenic ('cold') lesions with no increased radiotracer uptake at the sites of bone destruction. Which underlying condition is most classically associated with this finding?
items.e: Multiple myeloma features purely lytic bone destruction without significant osteoblastic activity, characteristically producing photopenic ('cold') lesions on a Tc-99m MDP bone scan. Osteosarcoma, prostate metastases, and Paget disease show intense increased osteoblastic radiotracer uptake ('hot' lesions).
items.note: Classic high-yield nuclear medicine question for orthopaedic exams.

items.q: On computed tomography (CT), tissue attenuation is measured in Hounsfield Units (HU). Which tissue is correctly paired with its standard HU value?
items.e: By definition, pure water has a CT attenuation value of 0 Hounsfield Units (HU). Air measures -1000 HU, fat measures -100 to -50 HU, and cortical bone measures +1000 HU or higher.
items.note: Factually flawless basic science question.

items.q: During musculoskeletal ultrasound of the patellar tendon, an artifactual hypoechoic area mimicking a partial tear is noted. Correcting the transducer angle so that the beam is perpendicular to the tendon fibres restores normal hyperechoic fibrillar architecture. This dynamic phenomenon is known as:
items.e: Anisotropy occurs when ultrasound sound waves interact with parallel tissue structures like tendons; when the beam is not perpendicular (90 degrees) to the fibres, returning signal is reduced, creating a falsely hypoechoic appearance that mimics tendinopathy or a tear.
items.note: Standard ultrasound physics concept tested frequently in orthopaedic board exams.

items.q: Which tissue interaction of X-rays dominates at lower photon energy levels and high atomic numbers, has a probability proportional to Z cubed / E cubed, and is primarily responsible for radiographic image contrast?
items.e: The photoelectric effect occurs when an incident X-ray photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron. Its probability is proportional to Z^3 / E^3, making it dominant at lower energies and higher atomic numbers (such as calcium in bone), providing image contrast and patient dose.
items.note: Core radiophysics question, completely accurate.

items.q: A 72-year-old male is scheduled for emergency hemiarthroplasty for a femoral neck fracture. He suffered a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago and has ongoing severe systemic cardiovascular disease that poses a constant threat to life. Which ASA physical status rating best classifies this patient?
items.e: ASA IV is defined as a severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, such as a recent myocardial infarction within 3 months. The suffix 'E' denotes emergency surgery.
items.note: Accurate, clear scenario directly testing ASA classification and emergency modifier according to consensus guidelines.

items.q: During a prolonged 5-hour total hip arthroplasty, 2 g IV cefazolin was administered 30 minutes prior to skin incision. Surgical blood loss at 4 hours is 600 mL. What is the correct timing for redosing cefazolin during this operation?
o: Redose at 4 hours after the initial dose
Redose only if blood loss exceeds 1500 mL
No redosing is required for surgeries under 6 hours
items.e: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis with cefazolin should be redosed every 4 hours during surgery, or after intraoperative blood loss exceeding 1500 mL.
items.note: Factually accurate and tests standard surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis protocols.

items.q: According to the ASRA guidelines, what is the minimum recommended duration that prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be held prior to performing a spinal anaesthesia block?
items.e: According to ASRA guidelines, a minimum of 12 hours must elapse between the last prophylactic dose of LMWH and spinal/epidural needle placement or catheter removal. For therapeutic LMWH, 24 hours is required.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer question testing standard neuraxial anaesthesia safety intervals.

items.q: A patient undergoing a minor orthopaedic procedure under local infiltration develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, and subsequent seizures due to local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Along with supportive care and airway management, which medication is specifically indicated?
items.e: Intravenous 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by infusion) is the specific rescue antidote for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST).
items.note: Standard, essential pharmacology question with distinct and plausible distractors.

items.q: Which of the following clinical signs is recognized as the earliest indicator of malignant hyperthermia in a patient undergoing general anaesthesia with volatile agents?
items.e: The earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia is an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, accompanied by tachycardia and masseter spasm. Hyperthermia is a late sign.
items.note: Standard high-yield intraoperative emergency question.

items.q: Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin used for severe osteoporosis. Based on findings from the ARCH trial, romosozumab is contraindicated in patients with which of the following conditions within the preceding 12 months?
items.e: Data from the ARCH trial indicated an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events with romosozumab, leading to the recommendation to avoid its use in patients who have had a myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year.
items.note: Well-formulated question testing landmark trial evidence and black-box safety warnings of bone-active agents.

items.q: According to the 2022 ACR/AAHKS guidelines, how should Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (such as tofacitinib or baricitinib) be managed prior to elective total knee arthroplasty in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Withheld for 3 days prior to surgery
Withheld for 2 weeks prior to surgery
Withheld for 4 weeks prior to surgery
items.e: The 2022 ACR/AAHKS perioperative guidelines recommend withholding targeted synthetic DMARDs (JAK inhibitors like tofacitinib and baricitinib) for 3 days prior to elective total joint arthroplasty.
items.note: Tests clear modern clinical practice consensus guideline timing.

items.q: During cemented hip hemiarthroplasty, a patient experiences a 45% drop in systolic blood pressure accompanied by severe hypoxia (SpO2 86%), but does not suffer cardiovascular collapse requiring CPR. According to the Donaldson criteria, this Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS) is classified as:
items.e: Donaldson Grade 2 BCIS is characterized by severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%), severe hypotension (fall in SBP > 40%), or unexpected loss of consciousness. Grade 3 involves cardiovascular collapse requiring CPR.
items.note: Accurately tests the universally cited Donaldson classification of BCIS.

items.q: Which of the following ligaments is considered the strongest in the human body and is the primary determinant of posterior pelvic ring stability?
items.e: The posterior sacroiliac ligaments are the strongest ligaments in the body. Posterior ligamentous stability is more critical for the integrity of the pelvic ring than anterior stability.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the strongest ligament and its role in pelvic stability as per the reference notes.

items.q: A surgeon performing a modified Stoppa approach for an acetabular fracture identifies a vascular connection between the external iliac and obturator systems located behind the superior pubic ramus. This vessel, which must be protected or ligated, is the:
items.e: The corona mortis is an anastomosis between the external iliac/inferior epigastric and obturator vessels. It is located behind the superior pubic ramus, approximately 4-6 cm from the symphysis, and is at risk during anterior pelvic approaches.
items.note: The question accurately describes the anatomy and clinical significance of the corona mortis.

items.q: A 35-year-old male is brought to the ER after a high-energy crush injury. Radiographs show a pubic symphysis diastasis of 4.5 cm and complete disruption of both the anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments. According to the Young-Burgess classification, this injury is associated with:
o: The lowest risk of associated head and chest injuries
Isolated rotational instability with vertical stability
The highest blood loss and transfusion requirements
Successful management with a pelvic binder placed at the iliac crests
items.e: Anteroposterior Compression Type III (APC III) involves complete disruption of the SI joint (both anterior and posterior ligaments). It is both rotationally and vertically unstable and is associated with the highest transfusion needs among pelvic injuries.
items.note: The question correctly links the injury pattern (APC III) to its clinical implications and uses a valid distractor regarding binder placement (which should be at the trochanters).

items.q: On a pelvic radiograph, an avulsion fracture of the L5 transverse process is a critical diagnostic clue indicating which of the following?
items.e: An L5 transverse process avulsion suggests the presence of vertical shear forces (Vertical Shear injury) and complete instability of the hemipelvis, as the iliolumbar ligaments are disrupted.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the clinical significance of the L5 transverse process avulsion as a marker for vertical instability.

items.q: Which Judet radiographic view is most appropriate to evaluate the integrity of the anterior column and the posterior wall of the acetabulum?
items.e: The obturator oblique view (45-degree oblique) best visualizes the anterior column and the posterior wall. The iliac oblique view best shows the posterior column and the anterior wall.
items.note: The question correctly tests the standard interpretation of Judet views.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient has a displaced acetabular fracture. Radiographic evaluation shows the 'spur sign' on the obturator oblique view. This finding is diagnostic of which Letournel pattern?
items.e: The spur sign is seen in both-column fractures; it represents the intact portion of the ilium (attached to the axial skeleton) projecting above the displaced articular segments.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the pathognomonic radiographic sign for both-column acetabular fractures.

items.q: According to Matta's roof arc measurements, non-operative management of a displaced acetabular fracture (excluding both-column and posterior wall types) may be considered if:
o: The medial roof arc is 30 degrees
The posterior roof arc is 40 degrees
All three roof arcs (medial, anterior, and posterior) are over 45 degrees
The fracture is a both-column type with secondary congruence
items.e: Roof arcs over 45 degrees on AP and Judet views indicate that the weight-bearing dome is intact and the joint is congruent, which may allow for non-operative treatment in specific fracture types.
items.note: The question correctly applies the numerical threshold for Matta's roof arcs and distinguishes it from other non-operative criteria.

items.q: A patient sustains a posterior hip dislocation with an associated femoral head fracture located cephalad (superior) to the fovea centralis. According to the Pipkin classification, this is a:
o: Type I fracture; usually managed non-operatively
Type II fracture; usually requires ORIF
Type III fracture; associated with a femoral neck fracture
Type IV fracture; associated with an acetabular fracture
items.e: A Pipkin Type II fracture is a femoral head fracture located superior (cephalad) to the fovea centralis. Because this involves the weight-bearing surface, ORIF is typically required to restore the articular surface.
items.note: The question correctly classifies the Pipkin fracture based on its anatomical location relative to the fovea and identifies the standard management.

items.q: A 70-year-old presents with a displaced femoral neck fracture. Which vessel provides the primary blood supply to the femoral head that is at risk in this intracapsular injury?
o: Lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery
Ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
items.e: The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), specifically its lateral epiphyseal (retinacular) branches, provides the main blood supply to the adult femoral head. Intracapsular fractures disrupt these vessels, leading to high risks of AVN and non-union.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the applied anatomy of the proximal femur as described in Campbell's and the provided notes.

items.q: A 30-year-old male sustains a high-energy femoral neck fracture with a fracture line angle of 60 degrees from the horizontal. According to the Pauwels classification, this fracture pattern is associated with:
o: Low risk of non-union due to dominant compression forces
A Pauwels Type II pattern which is inherently stable
High vertical shear forces and the highest risk of fixation failure
Minimal risk of displacement due to its valgus impacted nature
items.e: Pauwels Type III fractures have an angle over 50 degrees from the horizontal. They represent vertical shear patterns with the highest risk of non-union and fixation failure in young patients compared to more horizontal Type I and II fractures.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the Pauwels classification thresholds and the clinical implications of vertical shear in young patients.

items.q: An 80-year-old woman with a displaced (Garden IV) femoral neck fracture is medically fit, cognitively intact, and was walking independently outdoors prior to the injury. According to NICE guidelines and the HEALTH trial, what is the preferred management?
items.e: NICE recommends total hip arthroplasty (THA) for patients who are medically fit, not cognitively impaired, and walk independently outdoors with no more than one stick. The HEALTH trial showed small functional gains with THA over hemiarthroplasty in active patients.
items.note: The question accurately applies current evidence-based guidelines (NICE) and major trial results (HEALTH) for elderly hip fracture management.

items.q: A 65-year-old presents with a reverse oblique intertrochanteric fracture (AO/OTA 31A3). Why is a sliding dynamic hip screw (DHS) considered contraindicated for this specific fracture pattern?
o: It causes excessive impaction and shortening
It leads to medial displacement of the femoral shaft fragment
It cannot be combined with a lateral trochanteric side plate
It increases the risk of bone cement implantation syndrome
items.e: In reverse oblique fractures, the fracture line runs from the lateral cortex downwards and medially. A DHS is contraindicated because the shaft fragment tends to slide medially along the lag screw axis, leading to fixation failure. A cephalomedullary nail is preferred.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the mechanical failure mode of DHS in reverse oblique fractures as per AO principles and the provided notes.

items.q: In a subtrochanteric femur fracture, the proximal fragment is typically flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the flexion component of this deformity?
items.e: The iliopsoas attaches to the lesser trochanter and flexes the proximal fragment. The gluteus medius/minimus abduct it, and the short rotators externally rotate it, making reduction challenging.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific muscle responsible for the flexion component of the subtrochanteric fracture deformity.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman on long-term bisphosphonate therapy presents with lateral cortical 'beaking' and a transverse subtrochanteric fracture after minimal trauma. All of the following are characteristic features or management steps for this injury EXCEPT:
o: Imaging the contralateral femur to look for bilateral involvement
Stopping the bisphosphonate therapy and considering teriparatide
Prophylactic intramedullary nailing if a visible fracture line exists
The fracture is typically highly comminuted with multiple fragments
items.e: According to ASBMR criteria, atypical femoral fractures (AFF) are non-comminuted. They are typically transverse or short oblique with a medial spike and lateral cortical beaking. They are often bilateral and associated with prodromal pain.
items.note: The question correctly tests the ASBMR diagnostic criteria for atypical femoral fractures, specifically the lack of comminution.

items.q: A patient presents with a high-energy femoral shaft fracture. Radiographic screening identifies a subtle vertical femoral neck fracture on the same side. Which of the following is true regarding the management of this combination?
o: The neck fracture is rarely missed on initial trauma radiographs
Anatomical reduction and fixation of the femoral neck should be prioritized
The shaft fracture should be fixed first to facilitate neck reduction
A retrograde nail for the shaft is contraindicated in this scenario
items.e: Ipsilateral neck and shaft fractures are high-energy injuries where the neck fracture is missed in 20-30% of cases. Management prioritizes the neck fracture (anatomical reduction) to prevent AVN. A retrograde nail for the shaft is a valid option when treating the neck separately.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the high miss rate and the priority of anatomical neck reduction in ipsilateral injuries.

items.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding coronal plane fractures of the femoral condyle (Hoffa fractures)?
o: They are extra-articular fractures classified as AO Type 33A
The medial condyle is more commonly involved than the lateral
They are best visualized on a lateral radiograph or CT scan
They are typically fixed with transverse lag screws from medial to lateral
items.e: Hoffa fractures are coronal plane partial articular fractures (AO Type 33B3). The lateral condyle is more commonly involved. They are often missed on AP views and require lateral views or CT; they are fixed with anteroposterior (AP) lag screws.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the classification, common location, imaging requirements, and fixation orientation for Hoffa fractures.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents following a high-energy motor vehicle accident with a medial tibial plateau fracture. On examination, the limb is swollen with a suspected Moore Type II fracture-dislocation. Which of the following is most accurate regarding this injury pattern?
o: It is the most common type of tibial plateau fracture, accounting for 70% of cases
The popliteal artery and peroneal nerve are at significant risk of injury
The mechanism is typically a low-energy valgus load with axial force
It is best managed with a single lateral locking plate
items.e: Schatzker Type IV (medial plateau) fractures are often high-energy fracture-dislocations (Moore classification) where the popliteal artery and peroneal nerve are at significant risk. Lateral plateau fractures (Schatzker II) are the most common.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the high-energy nature and neurovascular risks associated with medial plateau fracture-dislocations as per the reference notes.

items.q: When evaluating the anatomy and common injury patterns of the tibial plateau, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The lateral plateau is concave and lower than the medial plateau
The medial plateau is convex and frequently undergoes pure depression fractures
The lateral plateau is convex and higher than the medial plateau
The medial plateau is smaller and carries less load than the lateral plateau
items.e: The lateral plateau is convex and higher, while the medial plateau is concave, larger, and stronger as it carries more load. Lateral fractures are more common due to the typical valgus-axial load mechanism.
items.note: Correctly tests the fundamental anatomical differences between the medial and lateral plateaus which dictate fracture patterns.

items.q: A 50-year-old patient with a comminuted Ruedi-Allgower Type III pilon fracture has been in a spanning external fixator for 10 days. Which clinical finding is the most reliable indicator that the soft tissues are ready for definitive open reduction and internal fixation?
o: The presence of the 'wrinkle sign' on the anterior ankle
A minimum of 21 days has passed since the initial injury
The complete disappearance of all fracture blisters
items.e: The 'wrinkle sign' indicates that the inflammatory swelling has subsided enough to allow for safe surgical incision and closure without excessive tension, typically occurring 7–14 days after injury for the plateau and 7–21 days for the pilon.
items.note: The wrinkle sign is the gold-standard clinical marker for soft-tissue readiness in pilon and plateau surgery.

items.q: During intramedullary nailing of a proximal-third tibial shaft fracture, the surgeon must be vigilant to avoid characteristic malalignment. Which of the following deformities most commonly occurs at this fracture site?
items.e: Proximal-third tibial fractures are prone to valgus and procurvatum (apex anterior) deformities when treated with intramedullary nails; blocking (Poller) screws and semi-extended positioning can help prevent this.
items.note: This is a classic board-exam fact regarding the technical challenges of proximal tibia nailing.

items.q: A 38-year-old sustains a Schatzker Type II (split-depression) fracture of the lateral tibial plateau. Which of the following soft-tissue injuries is most frequently associated with this specific fracture pattern?
items.e: Lateral meniscus tears are the most common associated soft-tissue injury with lateral plateau fractures; they are often peripheral and can sometimes become incarcerated within the fracture site.
items.note: Matches the reference notes stating lateral meniscus tears are the commonest associated injury with lateral plateau fractures.

items.q: According to the classic Ruedi-Allgower principles for the surgical management of pilon fractures, what is the first step in the operative sequence?
o: Bone grafting of the metaphyseal defect
Application of a medial buttress plate
items.e: The Ruedi-Allgower principles follow a 4-step sequence: (1) restore fibular length, (2) reconstruct the articular surface, (3) bone graft the metaphyseal defect, and (4) buttress the medial tibia.
items.note: Tests the specific historical sequence of pilon reconstruction which remains a fundamental teaching point.

items.q: A CT scan of a bicondylar tibial plateau fracture reveals a large displaced posteromedial shear fragment. Which surgical approach and anatomical interval are most appropriate for buttress plating of this fragment?
o: Anterolateral approach through a submeniscal arthrotomy
Posteromedial (Lobenhoffer) approach between the medial gastrocnemius and pes anserinus
Posterior (Burks-Schaffer) approach between the biceps femoris and IT band
Anteromedial approach through the tibialis anterior muscle
items.e: The posteromedial approach (Lobenhoffer) uses the interval between the medial head of the gastrocnemius and the pes anserinus/semimembranosus to access and buttress posterior column fragments missed by standard lateral plates.
items.note: Correctly identifies the specific approach and interval for posterior column fragments as per the Luo three-column concept.

items.q: In the management of a depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture, which material is documented to offer the best resistance to post-operative subsidence of the elevated articular fragment?
items.e: Subchondral bone substitutes are used to support the elevated joint surface; calcium phosphate cement is noted to resist subsidence better than bone graft or other substitutes.
items.note: Directly supported by the reference notes regarding the use of subchondral bone substitutes.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete sustains an ankle fracture with lateral talar shift. According to the classic study by Ramsey and Hamilton, how much reduction in the tibiotalar contact area occurs with just 1 mm of lateral talar shift?
items.e: Ramsey and Hamilton demonstrated that 1 mm of lateral talar shift reduces the tibiotalar contact area by approximately 42%, which serves as the biomechanical basis for the requirement of anatomical reduction in ankle fractures.
items.note: The question tests a fundamental biomechanical fact in orthopaedic trauma that is explicitly mentioned in the reference notes and standard textbooks.

items.q: In the Lauge-Hansen classification system for ankle fractures, which of the following mechanisms is the most common, accounting for approximately 40-75% of cases?
items.e: Supination-External Rotation (SER) is the most common mechanism of ankle fracture. It corresponds to a Weber B pattern where the fibular fracture is short oblique or spiral at the level of the syndesmosis.
items.note: This is a high-yield epidemiological fact in orthopaedic exams, supported by the provided notes.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with an isolated Weber B lateral malleolus fracture. On initial non-weight-bearing radiographs, the medial clear space is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to determine if the fracture is stable for non-operative management?
o: Stress ultrasound of the deltoid ligament
items.e: According to the notes, weight-bearing radiographs are used to decide whether an isolated Weber B fracture is stable. A weight-bearing mortise view with a normal medial clear space indicates stability, even if a gravity stress view shows widening.
items.note: The question reflects current evidence-based practice (e.g., the AIM trial) mentioned in the reference notes regarding the assessment of ankle stability.

items.q: An ankle fracture-dislocation is found to be irreducible by closed means in the emergency department. Radiographs reveal the fibula is trapped behind the posterolateral tibia in the incisura. What is this specific injury pattern called?
items.e: A Bosworth fracture-dislocation involves the fibula becoming trapped behind the posterolateral tibia (incisura). It is typically irreducible by closed means and requires emergency open reduction.
items.note: This is a classic, eponym-based orthopaedic emergency pattern described in the notes.

items.q: A patient presents with a vertical fracture of the medial malleolus and associated impaction of the medial tibial plafond. This injury pattern is characteristic of which Lauge-Hansen mechanism?
items.e: Vertical medial malleolus fractures with medial plafond impaction are characteristic of Supination-Adduction (SAD) Stage II injuries. These require fixation of the vertical fragment and elevation of the impacted articular surface.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific fracture morphology associated with the SAD mechanism as per Lauge-Hansen.

items.q: During the internal fixation of an unstable ankle fracture, the surgeon performs a 'Cotton test' to assess syndesmotic stability. Which of the following defines a positive result for this test?
o: Medial clear space widening > 5 mm on external rotation stress
Lateral pull on the fibula with a bone hook resulting in > 2 mm widening
Tenderness at the syndesmosis upon squeezing the mid-calf
Fibular shortening resulting in a break in the 'dime sign'
items.e: The Cotton (hook) test is an intraoperative test where a lateral pull is applied to the fibula with a bone hook. Widening of more than 2 mm indicates syndesmotic instability.
items.note: The question tests the correct intraoperative technique and threshold for diagnosing syndesmotic injury.

items.q: Which nerve is most at risk during a standard lateral approach to the fibula, specifically as it pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve is at risk during the lateral approach. It pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm above the tip of the lateral malleolus and crosses the surgical field obliquely.
items.note: This is a critical anatomical fact for surgical safety in ankle ORIF, as noted in the reference material.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient with insulin-dependent diabetes and established peripheral neuropathy sustains an unstable bimalleolar ankle fracture. Which of the following is a recommended management principle for this patient?
o: Immediate weight bearing in a boot to prevent Charcot changes
Early hardware removal at 6 weeks post-operatively
Prolonged non-weight bearing for about double the usual time
Primary ankle arthrodesis for all diabetic fractures
items.e: Diabetic patients, especially those with neuropathy, have higher rates of complications. Recommended management includes 'super-construct' fixation and prolonged non-weight bearing, often double the time required for non-diabetic patients.
items.note: The question addresses the specific management modifications required for high-risk diabetic patients, which is a common exam topic.

items.q: Based on recent anatomical studies by Hettrich et al. (2010), which vessel is the predominant source of blood supply to the humeral head, providing approximately 64% of its perfusion?
o: Ascending branch of the profunda brachii
items.e: While the anterior humeral circumflex and its arcuate branch were classically considered the main supply, modern studies (Hettrich, 2010) show the posterior humeral circumflex artery provides the majority (64%) of the blood supply to the humeral head.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the shift in anatomical understanding mentioned in the reference notes and standard textbooks like Campbell's.

items.q: According to Hertel's criteria, which radiographic parameter is considered a strong predictor of humeral head ischaemia following a proximal humerus fracture?
o: Posteromedial metaphyseal extension of the head fragment less than 8 mm
Presence of a valgus-impacted four-part pattern
Medial hinge displacement of less than 2 mm
items.e: Hertel identified that a short metaphyseal extension (< 8 mm) and a disrupted medial hinge (> 2 mm displacement) are significant predictors of head ischaemia, though ischaemia does not always result in avascular necrosis.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific thresholds (8mm and 2mm) defined by Hertel for predicting ischemia.

items.q: A 75-year-old woman sustains a displaced two-part surgical neck fracture of the humerus. According to the results of the ProFHER trial (2015), what is the recommended management strategy for this patient?
o: Non-operative management with a sling and early exercises
items.e: The ProFHER trial demonstrated that in elderly patients with displaced surgical-neck-involving fractures, there was no significant functional benefit of surgery over non-operative care at 2 and 5 years.
items.note: The ProFHER trial is a landmark study in orthopaedic trauma, and its findings are a common topic in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 45-year-old manual labourer presents with an isolated fracture of the lateral third of the clavicle. Radiographs show the fracture is medial to the coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments, with the medial fragment detached from the ligaments. This injury is classified as Neer Type II. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Sling immobilization as most heal uneventfully
Surgical fixation because of a high risk of non-union
items.e: Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures involve a disruption where the CC ligaments stay with the distal fragment while the proximal fragment is displaced; this pattern has a high non-union rate (approximately 30%) and typically requires surgical fixation.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the high non-union rate of Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures and the resulting surgical indication.

items.q: A patient presents with a shoulder injury following a fall. Physical examination reveals a prominent distal clavicle. An axillary lateral radiograph shows the distal clavicle is displaced posteriorly into the trapezius muscle. What is the Rockwood classification for this injury?
items.e: Rockwood Type IV acromioclavicular joint injuries are characterized by posterior displacement of the clavicle into or through the trapezius muscle, which is best visualized on an axillary lateral radiograph.
items.note: The question tests the specific diagnostic feature (posterior displacement) of Rockwood Type IV AC joint injuries.

items.q: Which of the following is an absolute indication for surgical fixation of a midshaft clavicle fracture?
items.e: Absolute indications for clavicle ORIF include open fractures, neurovascular injury, and skin tenting with impending perforation. Shortening > 2 cm and 100% displacement are relative indications supported by the COTS trial to reduce non-union.
items.note: The question distinguishes between absolute and relative indications for clavicle surgery, which is a standard exam distinction.

items.q: A 35-year-old man sustains a closed transverse midshaft humeral fracture in a motor vehicle accident. On examination, he has a complete radial nerve palsy. What is the most appropriate initial management of the nerve palsy?
o: Immediate surgical exploration of the radial nerve
Functional bracing of the humerus and observation of the nerve
Early EMG/NCV studies at 1 week to assess prognosis
Tendon transfers for wrist and finger extension
items.e: Radial nerve palsy associated with a closed humeral shaft fracture is typically a neurapraxia with a high rate of spontaneous recovery (70-90%). The recommended management is observation for 3-4 months before considering exploration or EMG.
items.note: The question tests the standard management protocol for radial nerve palsy in closed humeral fractures, emphasizing observation over immediate surgery.

items.q: A 60-year-old male sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation which is reduced in the emergency department. One week later, he reports persistent weakness in shoulder abduction. What is the most likely cause of this weakness in this age group?
items.e: In patients over 40 years of age, the incidence of rotator cuff tears following an anterior shoulder dislocation increases significantly. Persistent weakness after reduction in an older patient should be evaluated for a cuff tear via MRI or ultrasound.
items.note: The question highlights a critical clinical pearl regarding shoulder dislocations in the elderly population.

items.q: A 76-year-old female sustains a highly comminuted distal humerus fracture (AO/OTA 13C3) with poor bone quality. According to the provided notes, if a primary total elbow arthroplasty is performed, what lifelong lifting restriction should the patient be counselled on?
o: No lifting more than 10 kg as a single effort
No lifting more than 1 kg repeatedly
No lifting more than 10 kg repeatedly
No lifting more than 5 kg repeatedly
items.e: For elderly patients with unreconstructable 13C3 fractures treated with total elbow arthroplasty, lifelong lifting restrictions are roughly 1 kg for repetitive tasks and about 5 kg for a single lift.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the specific lifting restrictions mentioned in the reference notes for TEA.

items.q: During the surgical management of a 'terrible triad' injury of the elbow, which of the following reflects the correct sequence of stabilization when using a lateral approach?
o: Radial head replacement -> LUCL repair -> Coronoid fixation
Coronoid fixation -> Radial head fixation/replacement -> LUCL repair
LUCL repair -> Radial head replacement -> MCL repair -> Coronoid fixation
MCL repair -> LUCL repair -> Radial head fixation
items.e: The recommended sequence for terrible triad injuries is (1) coronoid fixation or anterior capsule repair, (2) radial head fixation or replacement, (3) LCL (LUCL) repair, and finally (4) MCL repair or external fixator if still unstable.
items.note: The sequence matches the O'Driscoll/standard surgical protocol described in the notes.

items.q: A 40-year-old patient presents with a comminuted radial head fracture. Clinical examination and imaging suggest an associated interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) tenderness. Which procedure is strictly contraindicated in this patient?
o: Stabilization of the DRUJ with K-wires
items.e: In an Essex-Lopresti injury (radial head fracture + IOM disruption + DRUJ injury), the radial head must never be excised as it is a critical longitudinal stabilizer. It must be fixed or replaced.
items.note: The question tests a critical 'never-event' in forearm trauma management as specified in the notes.

items.q: To protect the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) while utilizing the Kocher approach (between anconeus and ECU) for a radial head fracture, the surgeon should maintain the forearm in which position?
items.e: Pronating the forearm moves the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) anteriorly and medially, away from the surgical field in lateral approaches like Kocher and Kaplan.
items.note: This is a standard surgical pearl for lateral elbow approaches mentioned in the notes.

items.q: A patient undergoes ORIF with a 3.5 mm LC-DCP for a distal-third radial shaft fracture. Intraoperative testing reveals that the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) is reducible but remains unstable even when the forearm is placed in full supination. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform an open reduction of the DRUJ to check for ECU interposition
Pin the radius to the ulna with the forearm in supination
Apply a volar buttress plate to the distal ulna
Immediate active range of motion exercise
items.e: According to the notes, if the DRUJ is reducible but remains unstable after radial fixation, the radius should be pinned to the ulna in supination. If it were stable in supination, early motion would be the next step.
items.note: The original stem stated the DRUJ was stable in supination, which according to the notes would indicate early motion rather than pinning. I fixed the stem to justify the marked answer 'Pin'.

items.q: A 52-year-old active woman sustains a distal radius fracture after a fall. Post-reduction radiographs show a radial height of 11 mm, a radial inclination of 18 degrees, and a dorsal tilt of 5 degrees. Based on acceptable radiographic parameters for an active adult, which of the following is correct?
o: The radial height indicates excessive shortening.
The alignment is within acceptable limits.
The dorsal tilt is unacceptable and requires re-reduction.
items.e: Acceptable parameters after reduction in an active adult include shortening under 3-5 mm (normal height is 11-12 mm), radial inclination over 15 degrees, and dorsal tilt under 10 degrees (or neutral/volar tilt).
items.note: The question accurately tests the specific thresholds for acceptable reduction in distal radius fractures as per the provided reference notes.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with pain in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. Initial radiographs are negative, but an MRI confirms an undisplaced fracture of the scaphoid waist. According to the results of the SWIFFT trial (2020), what is the most appropriate management?
o: Percutaneous headless compression screw fixation to allow early return to work
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a volar approach
Above-elbow cast immobilization for 6 weeks followed by a brace
items.e: The SWIFFT trial (2020) showed no long-term functional or clinical benefit of early surgical fixation over cast immobilization for undisplaced or minimally displaced (under 2 mm) scaphoid waist fractures.
items.note: The question correctly applies the findings of the SWIFFT trial mentioned in the reference notes regarding scaphoid waist fractures.

items.q: Which of the following is a primary predictor of instability in distal radius fractures according to the Lafontaine criteria?
items.e: Lafontaine's instability predictors include dorsal angulation >20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular involvement, associated ulnar fracture, and age over 60. Initial shortening >5 mm is also a predictor.
items.note: The question accurately lists the Lafontaine criteria as provided in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient presents with a 'spilled teacup' appearance on a lateral wrist radiograph after a high-energy injury. This finding is characteristic of which Mayfield stage of perilunate instability?
items.e: Mayfield Stage IV represents a volar lunate dislocation, where the lunate is displaced and tilted volarly, resembling a spilled teacup on the lateral view. Stage I is scapholunate disruption, Stage II is lunocapitate, and Stage III is lunotriquetral disruption (perilunate dislocation).
items.note: The question correctly identifies the Mayfield classification stages and the specific radiographic sign for Stage IV.

items.q: A 45-year-old carpenter undergoes volar locking plate fixation for a comminuted distal radius fracture. Intraoperative imaging shows the plate is positioned distal to the 'watershed line'. Which complication is most likely to occur?
items.e: Placing a volar plate distal to the watershed line increases the risk of FPL tendon irritation and rupture due to plate prominence. EPL rupture is more common after undisplaced fractures (attrition at Lister's tubercle) or from long screws protruding dorsally.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific tendon at risk when a volar plate is placed too distally, as noted in the reference text.

items.q: In the natural history of both Scaphoid Non-union Advanced Collapse (SNAC) and Scapholunate Advanced Collapse (SLAC), which joint is typically spared from degenerative changes?
items.e: Both SNAC and SLAC patterns of wrist arthritis characteristically spare the radiolunate joint, which is why procedures like proximal row carpectomy or four-corner fusion are viable options.
items.note: The question tests a fundamental concept in carpal collapse patterns that is explicitly mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A 32-year-old gymnast presents with chronic wrist pain and is diagnosed with Kienböck disease. Radiographs show lunate sclerosis and collapse, and the PA view reveals a 'cortical ring sign' of the scaphoid, indicating fixed rotation. What is the Lichtman stage?
items.e: Lichtman Stage IIIB is characterized by lunate collapse associated with fixed scaphoid rotation (ring sign on PA view, radioscaphoid angle >60 degrees). Stage IIIA has lunate collapse but normal carpal alignment.
items.note: The question accurately differentiates between Lichtman stages IIIA and IIIB based on the presence of fixed scaphoid rotation.

items.q: Regarding the vascular anatomy of the scaphoid, which statement is true?
o: The proximal pole receives its primary blood supply from the superficial palmar branch.
Approximately 80% of the scaphoid is covered by articular cartilage.
The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters at the proximal pole.
Volar pole fractures have the highest risk of avascular necrosis.
items.e: The scaphoid is 80% covered by cartilage. Its blood supply is primarily retrograde from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery entering at the waist/dorsal ridge, making the proximal pole vulnerable to AVN following a fracture.
items.note: The question tests anatomical facts regarding scaphoid vascularity and cartilage coverage as detailed in the reference notes.

items.q: A 26-year-old polytrauma patient with bilateral femur fractures and a severe pulmonary contusion undergoes temporary spanning external fixation on admission. In the ICU, the patient improves. According to damage control orthopaedics (DCO) principles, which time window is considered optimal for definitive conversion to intramedullary nailing, and which period should strictly be avoided?
o: Optimal window is within days 2–4; avoid days 4/5–10/14
Optimal window is days 4/5–10/14; avoid days 2–4
Optimal window is within 24–48 hours; avoid days 5–7
Optimal window is after day 14; avoid days 1–3
items.e: In damage control orthopaedics, definitive conversion is performed during the 'window of opportunity' between days 4/5 and 10/14 once physiology recovers. Days 2–4 must be avoided because the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) peaks, increasing the risk of ARDS and multiple organ failure from a 'second hit'.
items.note: Correct timing

items.q: Regarding wound irrigation during the initial operative debridement of open fractures, the Fluid Lavage of Open Wounds (FLOW) trial demonstrated that:
o: High-pressure irrigation with castile soap significantly reduces deep infection rates compared to saline
High-pressure pulsatile lavage is significantly superior to low-pressure irrigation in reducing reoperation rates
Castile soap solution resulted in higher reoperation rates than normal saline, and low-pressure irrigation was equivalent to high-pressure irrigation
Normal saline combined with bacitracin additive under high pressure yields the lowest complication rates
items.e: The FLOW trial demonstrated that irrigating open fracture wounds with castile soap was worse than normal saline (higher reoperation rate), and that low-pressure irrigation was statistically equivalent in efficacy to high-pressure irrigation while being less expensive.
items.note: Matched trial results

items.q: A 24-year-old male undergoes intramedullary nailing of a closed tibial shaft fracture. Six hours postoperatively, he complains of severe leg pain out of proportion to the injury, markedly increased by passive stretch of the great toe. Distal dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. His blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Anterolateral compartment pressure measured with a slit catheter is 36 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Immediate emergent four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg
Elevate the limb above the heart and monitor compartment pressures hourly
CT angiography to investigate potential anterior tibial artery occlusion
Administer IV regional block and reassess in 2 hours
items.e: Delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure) is 60 - 36 = 24 mmHg. A delta pressure under 30 mmHg confirms acute compartment syndrome and mandates urgent fasciotomy; distal pulses are typically preserved until very late.
items.note: Delta pressure rule

items.q: Regarding severe open lower limb injuries and the indications for limb salvage versus primary amputation established by the Lower Extremity Assessment Project (LEAP) study, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Loss of plantar sensation at initial presentation is an absolute indication for primary amputation
Limb salvage demonstrates significantly superior functional outcomes (Sickness Impact Profile) at 2 and 7 years compared to amputation
A Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) of 7 or higher reliably predicts the need for amputation and should be used as the sole decision criterion
Absent plantar sensation at presentation does not mandate amputation, as approximately half of these limbs regain sensation by 2 years
items.e: The LEAP study demonstrated that initial plantar insensation is not an absolute indication for amputation, as about half of initially insensate limbs regain sensation by 2 years. Furthermore, salvage and amputation resulted in comparable functional outcomes (Sickness Impact Profile) at 2 and 7 years.
items.note: Correct LEAP finding

items.q: A 32-year-old motorcyclist sustains a high-energy knee dislocation associated with a Schatzker type IV tibial plateau fracture. The foot is cold and pulseless with a warm ischaemia time of 4.5 hours. Hard signs of popliteal arterial rupture are confirmed. What is the correct surgical sequence of management?
o: Definitive end-to-end vascular repair, definitive plate osteosynthesis, then wound closure without fasciotomy
Insertion of a temporary vascular shunt, skeletal stabilisation, definitive vascular reconstruction, and prophylactic fasciotomy
Definitive plate osteosynthesis first to provide a stable bed, followed by arterial grafting and primary wound closure
Four-compartment prophylactic fasciotomy first, followed by external fixation and then delayed vascular reconstruction
items.e: In limbs with warm ischaemia approaching or exceeding 4–6 hours, restoring blood flow rapidly with a temporary intraluminal shunt takes precedence. Once perfusion is restored, skeletal stabilisation is performed, followed by definitive vascular repair and routine prophylactic fasciotomy upon reperfusion.
items.note: Sequence per guidelines

items.q: Which strain range defined by Perren’s theory allows for secondary (indirect) bone healing?
items.e: Perren’s strain theory states that strains between 2 % and 10 % promote secondary bone healing with callus formation.

items.q: Primary (direct) bone healing demands the lowest interfragmentary strain. What condition is most likely to be met?

Any gap if fixation is rigid
Gap ≤1 mm with a bridging plate
items.e: Primary healing requires absolute stability, achieved when the fracture gap is ≤0.01 mm and interfragmentary compression is present.
